analysis.one_liner: Lets generic drug makers sue to strike patent claims that brand-name drug companies use to delay cheaper generics.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by a Democrat and a Republican with two Republican cosponsors, died in the Senate health committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: When a drug company first wins FDA approval, it files public patent information ('use codes') listing patents that cover its drug. The FDA has said some drug companies file overly broad or vague claims there, which can hold up approval of cheaper generic versions. This bill would let generic makers go to court and force a brand-name company to correct or delete use codes that do not match real, approved patents. The bill was referred to the Senate health committee and never received any action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who buy prescription drugs, since faster generic and biosimilar competition generally brings prices down. Generic drug manufacturers also gain a legal tool against patent filings they view as inflated.

how_it_helps.text: Gives generic and biosimilar applicants a new cause of action to sue the brand-name drug holder for a court order correcting or deleting a use code that does not correspond to an approved drug or an approved method of use, or that is overly broad or inaccurate [S3].
Addresses a process the FDA itself has flagged: overbroad or ambiguous use codes can delay approval of generic drugs, and those codes are the public signal of what patents may block a generic [S2].
Overly broad method-of-use patent claims are one of the legal tools that keep cheaper generic versions off the market longer, so narrowing them helps drug prices come down sooner [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies, which could face lawsuits challenging their patent use-code filings and could lose some of the delay that broad filings buy them.

drawbacks.text: It adds new litigation: generic companies could sue brand-name holders over use codes, adding another round of patent-related lawsuits in an area already heavy with them [S3].
It addresses only one delay tactic — inflated use codes — and does nothing about the broader patent thickets, pay-for-delay deals, or other tactics that keep generics off the market [S2].
A court order to correct a use code does not invalidate a patent; a generic maker could still face patent infringement litigation afterward [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A narrow, targeted fix. It would give generic makers a way to challenge patent paperwork the FDA has said can delay approvals, at the cost of some additional lawsuits between drug companies. It is a modest step: it does not touch the larger set of patent strategies that delay generic competition, so the price relief for consumers would be real but limited.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate health committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 30, 2023, by Senator Hassan with Senator Braun, a Republican, as the second name on it [S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day [S5].
No further action appears in the record — no committee hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers are better off: the court challenge to their use-code filings was never created, so the option of broad or vague patent filings that can slow generic approval remains untouched. Consumers continue paying brand-name prices longer than the bill's sponsors intended to allow.

for.name: Sen. Maggie Hassan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to let generic makers sue over inflated patent use codes.

for.name: Sen. Mike Braun
for.what_they_did: Joined Hassan as the second name on the bill at introduction.

against.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: The bill sat in the committee he chaired for the remainder of the Congress; no hearing, markup, or floor vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: A Democratic senator introduced the bill with a Republican as the second name, and its only two cosponsors were Republicans; there is no recorded opposition, only committee inaction.

industries.note: The bill would expose their patent use-code filings to court challenge, cutting into a tactic the FDA has said can delay generic approval and keep prices high. The bill's death leaves their filings unchallengeable.
They would gain a lawsuit to force correction of use codes that overstate patent coverage, speeding their path to market. The bill never advanced, so they gained nothing.
